title: Living on the Edge of a Supermassive Black Hole

8 min read

Just now

--

The closest known star to the black hole at the center of the Milky-Way galaxy, Sagittarius A*, is orbiting at a peak speed of 8.3% the speed of light or 25,000 kilometers per second. At this speed, this star, labeled S301, traverses twice the Earth’s diameter in a second and would cross the Earth-Moon distance in 15 seconds. The black hole mass, equivalent to 4.3 million suns, would have ripped this star apart if it were ten times closer in, at roughly the Earth-Sun separation. The event horizon of the black hole, from where nothing can escape, is about ten times smaller, so no star or planet can survive tidal disruption before being swallowed by Sagittarius A*. If Earth were to approach this black hole, it would have been converted into a stream of gas well outside the event horizon.

Tidal disruption of Earth-mass planets is not unique to black holes. In fact, debris from tidal disruptions of rocky planets fills interstellar space. As discussed in a paper I co-authored with Morgan MacLeod here, gravitational tides rip apart rocky planets close to the most abundant stars which have about a tenth of the mass of the Sun. The rocky debris from planets destroyed by dwarf stars could explain the first recognized interstellar meteor, IM1. In 2023, I led a Pacific Ocean expedition that recovered meteoritic fragments in the crash site of IM1 and found a tenth of them to be consistent with an interstellar origin here. Recent isotope analysis of these fragments confirming their interstellar origin will be featured in a Netflix documentary to come out in spring 2027.

The tidal force at the outer edge of dwarf stars declines inversely with the square of their mass, and is unable to rip apart a rocky planet for stars more massive than half the mass of the Sun. Coincidentally, the tidal force at the event horizon of a black hole also scales inversely with the square of the black hole mass. The Earth is safe from tidal disruption near the event horizon of a black hole more massive than 100 million suns.

How far do we need to travel before finding such a gigantic black hole?

Remarkably, the nearest neighbor of the Milky-Way, the Andromeda galaxy, has a supermassive black hole M31* with a mass in the range of just above 100 million suns. As shown twenty years ago in a paper I co-authored with T.J. Cox, M31* will merge with Sagittarius A* in about 5 billion years and the merged galaxy, which I termed Milkomeda, will host a black hole with well over 100 million solar masses at its center.

As it turns out, black holes with over a billion solar masses already formed in the infant Universe, less than a billion years after the Big Bang. Their discovery is akin to finding giant babies in a delivery room. From the start of my career in astrophysics four decades ago, I worked out the way by which these black holes could have formed through the direct collapse of supermassive stars, as detailed in many papers I wrote with postdocs and students, including Fred Rasio here, Daniel Eisenstein here, Zoltan Haiman here, Volker Bromm here, Fabio Pacucci here and Devesh Nandal here.

How much fun would it be to live on a planet in a circular orbit near the edge of a supermassive black hole with more than 100 million solar masses?

If the planet were to orbit on the so-called photon sphere, at a radius of 1.5 times the event horizon around a non-spinning black hole, residents of the planet could potentially observe light that makes a full orbit around the black hole. For a spinning black hole, which drags spacetime with it, the photon sphere is broadened into a thick shell of orbits.

Unfortunately, a photon sphere orbit is not stable and the planet will quickly migrate inward and disappear into the event horizon — where its residents will be ripped apart by divergent gravitational tides at the central singularity, the ultimate serial killer.

The innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) for a non-spinning black hole is at 3 times its event horizon radius, namely 6GM/c², where G is Newton’s constant, M is the black hole mass and c is the speed of light. For a black hole with a 100 million solar masses, the ISCO is at roughly the Jupiter-Sun separation.

There are great benefits to living on a planet at the ISCO. By dispensing trash into the black hole on a carefully engineered accretion stream, one can get clean energy in return with an efficiency of 5.7% for converting rest mass to radiation. This efficiency is at least 6 times better than the most efficient nuclear reactor can give. For a spinning black hole, the opportunities are greater, as engineers can couple a device to the spin of the black hole and use it as a giant flywheel from which energy can be harnessed.

If the black hole spins, it drags the fabric of spacetime around with it like a spinning ball in thick honey. Inside a region called the ergo-sphere, it is impossible to remain stationary relative to distant stars, any spacecraft is forced to orbit in the direction of the black hole’s spin. Spinning black holes also pull the ISCO much closer to the event horizon if the planet orbits in the same direction as the spin.

Beauty salons can offer slower aging near the black hole, where time passes slower for the orbiting observer compared to someone far away. At the ISCO of a non-rotating black hole, a clock ticks at 70.7% the rate of a distant clock. Close enough to the horizon of a maximally spinning black hole, an hour in orbit could equal decades or centuries in the outside universe.

As the planet orbits at near-light speed, light from the distant universe appears concentrated into a bright, narrow cone directly in front of the observer. Last week, I taught this so-called relativistic aberration effect in my Harvard Astronomy class on “Radiative Processes in Astrophysics”. At its extreme manifestation, the incoming starlight is heavily blue-shifted into high-energy X-rays and gamma rays, while the view behind the observer stretches into dim, redshifted darkness. For astronomers, the black hole can be used as a giant gravitational lens, better than any telescope they can construct on their planet. In principle, it is possible to view the entire history of the Universe by harvesting cosmic photons that were trapped for a long time in orbit around the black hole.

To a distant observer, the black hole’s dark shadow appears much larger than its actual event horizon, by a factor of 2.6 for a non-spinning black hole. This silhouette was imaged first at Harvard’s Black Hole Initiative, for which I served as the founding director between 2016–2021.

Residents on a planet near the ISCO can use gravitational waves for communication. They also have many opportunities for fun activities, such as surfing away from an active black hole with light sails or catching a ride on relativistic jets emanating away from it.

A drift inward from the ISCO will make for a fascinating journey towards the black hole mouth. Inside the photon sphere, the normal outward fling of circular motion reverses direction. Leaving the planet on a rocket that fires its thrusters to orbit faster actually pulls the rocket inward toward the black hole instead of pushing it outward.

Living on a planet at the edge of a black hole allows travel agencies to offer the most expensive journeys to space tourists with a terminal illness. For those, there is no better hospice than the interior of the event horizon of the black hole. This region offers the ultimate manifestation of the Las Vegas experience: “What happens there, stays there!”
